claims.inference: Repeated moves toward stronger peers and away from a role (club leader) where he felt he could not yet perform at the level the role implied.
claims.alternative: Could reflect a learning drive (Type 5) or a desire for belonging among the best (Type 6/2). The parents line shows the choice had a cost.

claims.claim: At Stripe he found a pattern of single-minded building "working from wake until sleep" and wrote, "These are the times I feel most alive."
claims.passage: These are the times I feel most alive.
claims.inference: Aliveness located in high-output delivery against deadlines; speed and shipping over process.
claims.alternative: Startup norms reward exactly this; many engineers of different types describe flow this way. Fortune independently reports he often coded through the night.

claims.claim: His launch rule: a soft and a hard launch date; "I've never hit a soft launch date, but have never missed a hard one."
claims.passage: I've never hit a soft launch date, but have never missed a hard one.
claims.inference: Shipping over procedure: plans for slippage, protects the real deadline.
claims.alternative: A common engineering practice; not type-specific alone.

claims.claim: Stacking every 1:1 on Tuesdays left him completely burned out; after hiring VP Engineering Marc Hedlund he handed the 1:1s over.
claims.passage: completely burned out by the end of the day.
claims.inference: He chooses the activity where he is most effective and energized over the people-management role; the "first ever" vacation at about 26 fits a pattern repeated in 2024.
claims.alternative: Energy conservation and meeting fatigue ("a single meeting will kill productivity," S04) are also classic Type 5 markers. Introversion, not type, may explain them.

claims.claim: His first-ever vacation, to Hawaii, became a build: he holed up with engineers building CTF3.
claims.passage: a vacation (my first ever) to Hawaii, and then holed myself up with a few engineers building CTF3.
claims.inference: Rest that turns into building; matches the 2024 sabbatical pattern.
claims.alternative: He framed it as a tactic to route problems to Hedlund.

claims.claim: He admitted in 2014 to "having trouble distinguishing 'not the way I'd do it' from 'bad'."
claims.passage: having trouble distinguishing 'not the way I'd do it' from 'bad'
claims.inference: Candid self-criticism about judging others’ methods; the principle is notable because later colleagues describe him jumping into others’ projects and working around people (C33, C31).
claims.alternative: The judging habit is a Type 1 marker (the strongest alternative). The irony with later reports is interpretation; the later reports are anonymous and contested.

claims.claim: He defined "sparse micromanagement" as jumping in to some random issue, overturning all the decisions, and disappearing, and called it the worst.
claims.passage: jumping in to some random issue, overturning all the decisions, and then disappearing
claims.inference: His stated principle; later anonymous colleagues describe him taking things into his own hands (C33).
claims.alternative: The later reports are anonymous; the parallel is interpretation.

claims.claim: The 2014 essay ends: "What my role will look like from here, I have yet to define fully. I'm too busy coding."
claims.passage: I'm too busy coding.
claims.inference: Identity in output over role.
claims.alternative: A witty sign-off.

claims.claim: By late 2014 he had removed himself as a critical lynchpin at Stripe and could craft any role; he called it a "strangely luxurious place."
claims.passage: a strangely luxurious place: I'd successfully removed myself as a critical lynchpin for the company and could craft literally any role I wanted.
claims.inference: He celebrated being unneeded.
claims.alternative: Public announcement presents the exit favorably.

claims.claim: He left Stripe in May 2015 because he was "yearning to create something of my own" and did not want to "always wonder what could have been."
claims.passage: I was yearning to create something of my own.
claims.inference: A costly exit from a secure, prestigious role toward something "of my own" and bigger. Fits an achievement/significance drive; argues against a Type 2 need to be needed (he celebrated being unneeded).
claims.alternative: Also fits Type 7 (topped-out novelty) or simple ambition. The 2026 "not my problem" framing is retrospective.

claims.claim: Interpretation: a Type 2, whose worth rests on being needed, would be expected to stay where the need was; Brockman left once he was no longer the critical piece.
claims.passage: whose sense of worth rests on being needed, would be expected to stay where the need was.
claims.inference: Argues against Type 2.
claims.alternative: Also consistent with Type 7 restlessness or plain ambition.

claims.claim: After a July 2015 dinner in Menlo Park, he wrote that the project needed someone full-time and "I volunteered myself as tribute."
claims.passage: I volunteered myself as tribute.
claims.inference: Willingness to take any role in service of the project; shows role flexibility toward a goal.
claims.alternative: Self-effacing service also fits Type 2 or 9. The same posts present him as the indispensable organizer, so humility and centrality coexist.

claims.claim: When the team arrived at his apartment (the first office) and found no whiteboard, he got them one and other office supplies.
claims.passage: I quickly got them a whiteboard and any other office supplies they needed.
claims.inference: Unglamorous service in the role.
claims.alternative: Self-told anecdote.

claims.claim: He resolved to do whatever was needed to remove all non-research tasks from Ilya Sutskever's plate.
claims.passage: resolved to do whatever was needed to remove all non-research tasks from Ilya's plate
claims.inference: Role flexibility toward the goal.
claims.alternative: Also fits 9 or 2 self-effacement.

claims.claim: In January 2017 he wrote that he found his role "not by seeking it — instead, I sought out a problem more important to me than my role within it." The article quotes the second clause.
claims.passage: a problem more important to me than my role within it.
claims.inference: His stated hierarchy: mission over role, people over code.
claims.alternative: Public self-presentation written as a recruiting post; it can be read as a 9-like self-forgetting or a 3’s identification with the goal.

claims.claim: In 2015 he wrote of "the deep satisfaction of having others actually use my creations."
claims.passage: the deep satisfaction of having others actually use my creations.
claims.inference: A recurring, spontaneous vocabulary of validation tied to accomplishment registered by others: a core Type 3 marker when combined with C17.
claims.alternative: A Type 2 would also prize others’ appreciation; a healthy builder of any type enjoys users. Weight comes from the recurrence across 11 years, not any single line.

claims.claim: In 2017, after nights fixing bugs for night-owl researchers on Universe (Dario Amodei and Rafał Józefowicz), he wrote of "something extremely validating" about enabling researchers' questions.
claims.passage: something extremely validating about your work allowing researchers to ask questions that no human ever has before.
claims.inference: Validation vocabulary tied to others registering his work.
claims.alternative: Also service-oriented (Type 2) language.

claims.claim: In 2019 he wrote that the Dota team's excitement at each obstacle he overcame "was deeply validating."
claims.passage: the team's excitement every time I overcame a new obstacle was deeply validating.
claims.inference: Recurring validation vocabulary (with C16, C75, C07).
claims.alternative: Ordinary pleasure in team appreciation.

claims.claim: In the Dota work he felt "half blind" beside Jakub Pachocki and Szymon Sidor, who had made the core breakthrough powering the bot, and wanted to make critical contributions like theirs.
claims.passage: the core breakthrough that powered our Dota bot
claims.inference: Wanting the visible, critical contribution.
claims.alternative: Also a reasonable desire to understand the full stack ("see the whole picture").

claims.claim: In November 2018 he took "a gamble with three months of my time," self-studying over the holidays.
claims.passage: a gamble with three months of my time
claims.inference: Return to the skill in private.
claims.alternative: Workload had eased, a practical trigger.

claims.claim: He says, "I learn best when I have something specific in mind to build."
claims.passage: I learn best when I have something specific in mind to build.
claims.inference: Knowledge as instrumental; argues against Type 5.
claims.alternative: Self-description.

claims.claim: A new relationship sustained him: "someone who made me feel it was ok if I failed."
claims.passage: I'd begun a relationship with someone who made me feel it was ok if I failed.
claims.inference: Failure made safe and private; key to the 3 reading.
claims.alternative: Also fits a Type 6 need for safety before risk.

claims.claim: The relationship appears (by timing) to be with Anna, whom he married at OpenAI's office in November 2019 after about a year of dating; Sutskever officiated and a robotic hand was ring bearer.
claims.passage: That appears to be Anna, whom he married at OpenAI's office in November 2019 after about a year of dating
claims.inference: Identification is an inference from timing (first holiday season together late 2018; girlfriend of one year in Nov 2019).
claims.alternative: The essay does not name her; labeled "appears to be".

claims.claim: He describes the breakthrough as the moment "my frustration overwhelmed my fear," making a change that touched an entire model.
claims.passage: my frustration overwhelmed my fear
claims.inference: Fear named as the obstacle.
claims.alternative: Fear language also supports a Type 6 reading.

claims.claim: By mid-2019, with Pachocki and Sutskever advising, results drew Pachocki and Sidor to the project full time; "I feel proud every time I see a commit from them in the machine learning codebase I'd started."
claims.passage: I feel proud every time I see a commit from them in the machine learning codebase I'd started.
claims.inference: Pride in visible output and his role as originator.
claims.alternative: Generous credit to teammates as well.

claims.claim: He measured recovery in coding hours (about 75% of his historical level).
claims.passage: around 75% of the number of coding hours from where I've been historically.
claims.inference: Self-measurement by output metrics.
claims.alternative: Engineers commonly track hours; weak alone.

claims.claim: He concluded he had been "unwilling to become a beginner again."
claims.passage: I couldn't make the transition because I was unwilling to become a beginner again.
claims.inference: Image cost of beginner status.
claims.alternative: Lesson-shaped essay.

claims.claim: Interpretation: the essay shows the Type 3 fear of failing where people can see it.
claims.passage: That is the Type 3 fear in plain form: failing where people can see it.
claims.inference: Central discriminator from self-report without legal stakes.
claims.alternative: Type 5 and Type 6 partly explain it; essay ends with a hiring pitch.

claims.claim: Interpretation contrasting 1, 5 and 3: a One's block centers on doing it wrong; his centered on others' estimate and having a result to point to.
claims.passage: A One's block tends to center on doing it wrong; his centered on others' estimate of him and on having a result to point to.
claims.inference: Discriminator against Type 1.
claims.alternative: Typological generalization; one essay.

claims.claim: The 2019 essay ends with a hiring pitch ("apply to OpenAI!").
claims.passage: it ends with a hiring pitch ("apply to OpenAI!")
claims.inference: Limit on the essay as evidence.
claims.alternative: None.

claims.claim: In September 2017 Sutskever sent Musk and Altman an email signed "Greg & Ilya" admitting they had withheld concerns because "we were afraid of harming the relationship, having you think less of us, or losing you as partners," that they were "much worse at being a counterbalance" to Musk than Altman, that they had "allowed the idea of financial return 2-3 years down the line to drive our decisions," and "did not speak our full truth." Two days later they told Zilis they would continue as a nonprofit.
claims.passage: we were afraid of harming the relationship, having you think less of us, or losing you as partners
claims.inference: Jointly authored evidence of reluctance to confront a powerful partner and concern with how they were seen, then a costly confession.
claims.alternative: Cannot be assigned to Brockman alone. The fear of "harming the relationship" fits Types 9/6/2 as well as 3. Use cautiously and attribute to both.

claims.claim: Brockman's 2017 diary, produced in the Musk litigation and quoted by The New Yorker, includes "Happy to not become rich on this, so long as no one else is" and, answering "So what do I *really* want?", "Financially what will take me to $1B."
claims.passage: Happy to not become rich on this, so long as no one else is
claims.inference: Contemporaneous private evidence of conflicting instincts: wealth as a personal target, fairness/relative-wealth language, and a moral and reputational check on how the for-profit move would look.
claims.alternative: Outlets render wording differently (MIT TR: "Financially, what will take me to $1B?"); the article quotes The New Yorker's version. Musk's lawyers chose the excerpts.

claims.claim: The New Yorker quotes the diary answer "Financially what will take me to $1B."
claims.passage: Financially what will take me to $1B.
claims.inference: Personal financial target.
claims.alternative: Excerpt selected by opposing counsel; one line among conflicting entries.

claims.claim: A November 2017 diary entry, as MIT Technology Review rendered it, says converting to a b-corp without Musk would be "pretty morally bankrupt."
claims.passage: it'd be wrong to steal the nonprofit from him. to convert to a b-corp without him. that'd be pretty morally bankrupt.
claims.inference: Moral vocabulary (Type 1 case).
claims.alternative: Courthouse News renders the entry with different punctuation and an added clause.

claims.claim: Courthouse News's rendering of the same entry continues "and he's really not an idiot."
claims.passage: and he's really not an idiot
claims.inference: Practical risk sits beside the moral judgment.
claims.alternative: Wording differs across outlets; trial exhibit not opened.

claims.claim: On the stand in May 2026 he explained the entry: "I meant it would actually serve the mission, but it'd be hard to look at yourself in the mirror."
claims.passage: I meant it would actually serve the mission, but it'd be hard to look at yourself in the mirror.
claims.inference: His own gloss locates the 2017 obstacle in how the act would reflect on him ("look at yourself in the mirror") while conceding it would have served the goal. That fits an image-and-effectiveness frame better than a pure rule frame.
claims.alternative: A Type 1 also uses "mirror" language for conscience. Trial testimony is adversarial and lawyered.

claims.claim: He told the jury in May 2026, "Solving for the mission has always been my primary motivation."
claims.passage: Solving for the mission has always been my primary motivation.
claims.inference: Total identification with the mission. For the Type 3 reading, the mission is the goal his worth is fused with; for Type 1, it is a moral cause.
claims.alternative: Strong incentives: recruiting, PR and, at trial, a legal defense against greed claims. Consistency over time is real, but self-report cannot establish motive.

claims.claim: Interpretation: the diary establishes a tension between a personal financial target, a comparative fairness rule, and a line he would not cross alone; the mirror idiom fits either type.
claims.passage: What the diary does establish is the tension itself
claims.inference: Honest limit on the diary as type evidence.
claims.alternative: Excerpts chosen by opposing counsel.

claims.claim: The WSJ reports that after Musk left in 2018, Altman and Dario Amodei agreed employees lacked faith in Brockman and Sutskever's leadership, given layoffs.
claims.passage: agreed that the lab's employees didn't have faith in Brockman and Sutskever's leadership, given the layoffs.
claims.inference: Independent outlets converge on friction over his management by 2018.
claims.alternative: Sources are largely unnamed and include the Amodeis’ allies. The layoffs were requested by Musk (S22). Present as reported friction, not a finding.

claims.claim: When he sought a role on the language project, co-lead Daniela Amodei offered to step down rather than allow it; he and Altman reluctantly agreed to keep him off.
claims.passage: offered to step down as head of the project rather than allow Brockman on it.
claims.inference: He pushed to be where the frontier work was and appealed over a peer’s head; others resisted his involvement.
claims.alternative: Unnamed sourcing; Radford reportedly felt used in a proxy war. Brockman’s side is not given.

claims.claim: In March 2020 he wrote lengthy peer feedback accusing Daniela Amodei of abusing her power to create bureaucratic processes; Altman called it "tough but fair"; he later offered to withdraw it.
claims.passage: wrote a lengthy piece of feedback for Daniela accusing her of abusing her power to create bureaucratic processes to get her way
claims.inference: He attacked process as an obstacle (anti-bureaucracy), engaged conflict directly, then offered to retract when it escalated. Useful for the 1-versus-3 discriminator: he opposed procedure rather than defending it.
claims.alternative: The fairness charge ("abusing her power") is also Type 1 moral language. Unnamed sourcing; Daniela disputes his critique.

claims.claim: The New Yorker reports researchers chafed under Brockman, "whom some considered an abrasive operator."
claims.passage: whom some considered an abrasive operator.
claims.inference: Independent outlet converges on friction.
claims.alternative: Unnamed "some"; rival camp context.

claims.claim: Anonymous former OpenAI employees told Fortune he would "work around people if necessary" and is "an ends-over-means kind of person."
claims.passage: He's very much an ends-over-means kind of person.
claims.inference: Third-party convergence on results-first intensity and boom-bust work cycles. "Ends-over-means" directly discriminates against Type 1.
claims.alternative: Most quotes are anonymous; Su is a deal partner. Hard-driving pace also fits Types 8 and 7. Use as reported description with attribution.

claims.claim: A former engineer told Fortune he would "go super hard, then go off like a bear and hibernate for a few weeks."
claims.passage: He'd go super hard, then go off like a bear and hibernate for a few weeks, and then come back,
claims.inference: Boom-bust work cycle.
claims.alternative: Anonymous.

claims.claim: A former researcher told Fortune he has incredibly high standards and expects results.
claims.passage: He has incredibly high standards and expects results.
claims.inference: High standards fit both 1 and 3.
claims.alternative: Anonymous.

claims.claim: At about 200 employees, he set Slack to notify him of every message on every channel.
claims.passage: he had Slack notify him of every message on every channel.
claims.inference: Total involvement.
claims.alternative: Anonymous former engineer.

claims.claim: Sutskever sent the board a memo critical of Brockman before Altman's firing, confirmed under oath on October 1, 2025.
claims.passage: Sutskever sent the board a memo critical of Brockman, which he confirmed under oath on October 1, 2025
claims.inference: Documents that serious internal complaints existed; their content is not public.
claims.alternative: Memo text not public; OpenAI denies the claims.
claims.review_trigger: Update if the Brockman memo is released, Hagey’s or Hao’s book passages are opened, or Murati/Sutskever speak on record.

claims.claim: Fortune reports that Keach Hagey's book suggested the memo laid out concerns about Brockman's "alleged bullying"; OpenAI told Fortune "These claims aren't true."
claims.passage: suggested it laid out concerns about Brockman's "alleged bullying."
claims.inference: Serious internal complaints existed.
claims.alternative: Book not opened; allegation unproven and denied. Not load-bearing.
claims.review_trigger: Update if the memo is released or the Hagey/Hao passages are opened.

claims.claim: OpenAI told Fortune: "These claims aren't true."
claims.passage: These claims aren't true.
claims.inference: Company denial.
claims.alternative: Interested party.
claims.review_trigger: Update with any new on-record response.

claims.claim: Sutskever testified that his written claim Brockman "was essentially fired from Stripe" rested on "Mira told me" and that he never verified it; Brockman's 2015 post and same-day reporting describe a voluntary exit.
claims.passage: rested on "Mira told me,"
claims.inference: Unverified hearsay, presented only as such.
claims.alternative: Murati has not spoken on record about it.
claims.review_trigger: Update if Murati or Brockman address the Stripe claim on record.

claims.claim: Interpretation: largely anonymous or rival-camp sources still converge on speed over process.
claims.passage: Still, separate outlets describe the same tendency: speed over process.
claims.inference: Convergence, not proof.
claims.alternative: Sources overlap in camp and anonymity.

claims.claim: On November 17, 2023, he recalls thinking "It just wasn't right" and, asked if it was anger, "No. I felt like I understood what had happened."
claims.passage: No. I felt like I understood what had happened.
claims.inference: His most consequential costly choice: giving up position and equity security in hours, in solidarity with Altman. Loyalty and a moral verdict ("wasn’t right"), with anger denied.
claims.alternative: Denying anger while judging something "not right" is a classic Type 1 pattern (also 9). Loyalty to the winning partner also fits pragmatic 3; he estimated a 10% chance of getting the company back and began planning a new company with Altman the same day.

claims.claim: The joint post that night says Greg was told he was being removed from the board but was vital and would retain his role, and that Sam had been fired; Sutskever had texted at 12:19 p.m.
claims.passage: Greg was told that he was being removed from the board (but was vital to the company and would retain his role) and that Sam had been fired.
claims.inference: Contemporaneous timeline.
claims.alternative: Their account.

claims.claim: He told his wife "Got to quit," and she said "I agree."
claims.passage: Right after I hung up the call, I talked to my wife and I said, 'Got to quit.' And she said, 'I agree.'
claims.inference: Costly choice made in hours.
claims.alternative: Retrospective, auto-captioned interview.

claims.claim: His note to staff, posted November 17, 2023: "but based on today's news, i quit," closing with belief in the mission.
claims.passage: but based on today's news, i quit
claims.inference: Documented resignation.
claims.alternative: None.

claims.claim: Interpretation: November 17 is the One reading's best day; nothing in it favors a Three over a One.
claims.passage: it is the One reading's best day
claims.inference: Honest concession.
claims.alternative: Loyalty also fits Six.

claims.claim: Karen Hao, embedded at OpenAI in 2019, found him "nervous and guarded" ("We’ve never given someone so much access before"); he "recites the charter like scripture," then volunteered that he knew the lines because he had pored over them "to get them exactly right. It’s not like I was reading this before the meeting." He drew heavily on heroic stories (the moon-shot janitor, the transcontinental railroad, Edison).
claims.passage: I guess I know all these lines because I spent a lot of time really poring over them to get them exactly right.
claims.inference: Close attention to how he comes across (pre-empting the impression of reading a script) alongside exacting precision about the mission text.
claims.alternative: The precision and scripture-like devotion are the strongest single support for the Type 1 alternative; nervousness with a reporter is situational.

claims.claim: Interpretation for the alternative: his moral vocabulary recurs—"pretty morally bankrupt" (2017 diary), "It just wasn't right" with anger denied (2023), the charter learned "exactly right" and recited "like scripture" (2019), his self-confessed habit of treating "not the way I’d do it" as "bad" (2014), and "encounter the hard truth" (2026)—which is the strongest case for Type 1.
claims.passage: Read this way, he is a reformer whose mission is a moral cause
claims.inference: Must be presented near the main type argument as the strongest alternative.
claims.alternative: Each item has a non-1 reading: the mirror gloss (C23) frames morality as self-image; ends-over-means and anti-bureaucracy (C32, C33) cut against 1.

claims.claim: Interpretation: the charter aside cuts both ways (One's care for exactness; Three's reflex to manage impression).
claims.passage: Even the charter aside cuts both ways
claims.inference: Original detail read both ways.
claims.alternative: Nervousness with a reporter is situational.

claims.claim: Interpretation/discriminator: Ones usually defend procedure; Brockman repeatedly sides with speed (launch rule, anti-bureaucracy charge, ends-over-means, mirror gloss).
claims.passage: Ones are usually the people defending procedure, and Brockman keeps turning up on the other side.
claims.inference: Core discriminator.
claims.alternative: Several items are anonymous, rival-sourced or lawyered.

claims.claim: He and his wife gave $25 million to MAGA Inc.; he committed $50 million to Leading the Future, a pro-AI super PAC that has funded opponents of candidates who favor AI regulation, while OpenAI's official stance is not to contribute to such PACs; OpenAI said his involvement was personal.
claims.passage: He and his wife gave $25 million to MAGA Inc., a pro-Trump super PAC, and he committed $50 million to Leading the Future
claims.inference: A bold, costly public bet followed by a reversal justified by the reputational cost to the company and colleagues, not by calling the giving wrong. Fits the effectiveness/image frame of the discriminator.
claims.alternative: Date of the MAGA Inc. gift varies across sources (New Yorker "this year"; Wikipedia 2025), so the article leaves it undated. Motive unknown; WIRED interview not opened.
claims.review_trigger: Re-check after the Nov. 3, 2026 midterms and any FEC filings or new statements from Brockman about either PAC; open the NYT report and the WIRED interview before quoting.

claims.claim: According to The New York Times as relayed by Gizmodo, in June 2026 he wrote on Slack that he felt terrible LTF kept "reflecting on the company" and becoming a distraction.
claims.passage: I also want to say that I feel terrible about the fact that LTF keeps reflecting on the company and become so much of a distraction for people here
claims.inference: Reversal justified by reputational cost to the company, not wrongness.
claims.alternative: Secondhand; NYT not opened.
claims.review_trigger: Open the NYT report to confirm wording; re-check after the Nov. 3, 2026 midterms.

claims.claim: Same Slack message: "We've donated $25m so far, and have no plans to donate more at this time."
claims.passage: We've donated $25m so far, and have no plans to donate more at this time.
claims.inference: Halfway through a $50M pledge.
claims.alternative: Secondhand; plans can change.

claims.claim: His fuller rationale for the donations, given to WIRED in February 2026, was not available for this profile.
claims.passage: His fuller rationale, given to WIRED in February 2026, was not available for this profile.
claims.inference: Honest limit.
claims.alternative: Opening WIRED could change the discriminator.
claims.review_trigger: Open the WIRED interview and revise if his own rationale frames the gifts or reversal in moral terms.

claims.claim: Interpretation: the Three reading rests on agreement between weaker items and the 2019 essay, written with no legal stakes.
claims.passage: The Three reading rests on their agreement with the 2019 essay, written with no legal stakes.
claims.inference: Convergence argument.
claims.alternative: The essay is recruiting copy.

claims.claim: He told Shane Parrish he approached OpenAI "through a lens of uncertainty," has worked to "have a stronger sense of self," and regrets times "we just waited too long."
claims.passage: through a lens of uncertainty, of feeling like I don't know what the right answer is
claims.inference: The strongest material for a Type 9 (or 6) reading: merging opinions, weak sense of self, avoided hard conversations.
claims.alternative: Leadership-lesson clichés suited to the podcast format and post-2023 narrative; they sit oddly with third-party accounts of him writing a harsh critique and working around people (C32, C33).

claims.claim: His lesson learned more than once: "Make the hard decision. Have the hard conversation."
claims.passage: Make the hard decision. Have the hard conversation.
claims.inference: Nine-like conflict avoidance acknowledged.
claims.alternative: Podcast rapid-fire cliché.

claims.claim: He calls Sutskever's departure maybe the only moment he did not want to continue.
claims.passage: maybe the only moment in OpenAI's history where I felt like I didn't want to do it anymore.
claims.inference: Nine years without a break, a collapse of motivation when a key partner left, then rest that was itself more building. Matches the "bear" cycle in C33.
claims.alternative: Fortune reports outlets tied the sabbatical to concerns about his leadership style; OpenAI says it was his decision (S19). Both may be true.

claims.claim: On August 5, 2024 he announced a sabbatical: "First time to relax since co-founding OpenAI 9 years ago."
claims.passage: First time to relax since co-founding OpenAI 9 years ago.
claims.inference: Nine years without rest.
claims.alternative: None.

claims.claim: Fortune reported media outlets linked the sabbatical to concerns that his demanding leadership style created team tension; OpenAI said it was his decision.
claims.passage: his demanding leadership style had created tension within teams
claims.inference: Reported context.
claims.alternative: OpenAI disputes the framing; both may be true.

claims.claim: During the sabbatical he trained DNA language models for the Arc Institute, work he calls personally meaningful to him and his wife, who he says has a lot of health conditions.
claims.passage: has a lot of health conditions
claims.inference: Rest that became building; personal stakes.
claims.alternative: Auto-captioned; health details are his to share and kept general.

claims.claim: He returned in November 2024: "longest vacation of my life complete. back to building @OpenAI."
claims.passage: longest vacation of my life complete. back to building @OpenAI.
claims.inference: Return framed as building.
claims.alternative: None.

claims.claim: He says moving from hands-on coding to leading "has been something for me that was difficult, because you had to let go of something that I was used to and valued and really loved. But I’ve actually replaced it with something I love even more," and, asked if he will ever have a 24-hour coding session again: "I hope so... but I will say that I have found so much joy and value in helping the team in the way that I do now."
claims.passage: But I've actually replaced it with something I love even more.
claims.inference: Shift of identity from maker to leader; joy relocated to the team’s output.

type_hypothesis.against: Real evidence resists Type 3. (1) Moral vocabulary recurs across a decade: "pretty morally bankrupt" in the November 2017 diary (C89), "It just wasn't right" with anger explicitly denied on the day he quit (C35), learning the charter "exactly right" and reciting it "like scripture" (C20), his 2014 admission that he treats "not the way I'd do it" as "bad" (C11), the "abusing her power" charge in his 2020 peer review as the WSJ describes it (C32), and "incredibly high standards" (C94). That is the Type 1 case (C52). (2) He repeatedly steps out of status roles: handing off management to code at Stripe (C10, C69), celebrating that he was no longer a "lynchpin" (C70), fetching whiteboards and taking non-research work off Sutskever's plate (C72, C73), finding his role "not by seeking it" (C15), and taking "a less public-facing role" after 2019 (C40). A classic image-driven 3 would be expected to hold the visible executive seat. (3) His 2026 self-account stresses uncertainty, a weak "sense of self," avoided hard conversations and waiting too long (C39, C110), and the jointly signed 2017 email admits withholding concerns for fear of "harming the relationship" (C25). That supports Type 9 or 6. (4) His loyalty on November 17, 2023 cost him position immediately and he became emotional about the loyalty others showed him (C35, C101, C36, C119), which fits 2/6 as well as 3. (5) Incentives explain much: startup and lab cultures reward all-night sprints; mission talk is recruiting, PR and, in May 2026, a legal defense against greed claims (C19, C23). (6) Much of the friction evidence is anonymous or comes from his rivals, the Amodeis (C30–C34, C92–C96), and some is disputed outright.
type_hypothesis.alternative_case: Type 1 is the strongest rival. It explains the moral and correctness language above, the devotion to a written charter he worked to get "exactly right" (C20), a reformer's conviction about the mission (C19), the judging habit he admits (C11), fairness language ("Happy to not become rich on this, so long as no one else is," C22; the "abusing her power" charge, C32), high standards (C94), the moral verdict and denied anger on November 17 (C35), and the self-control of working nine years without rest (C111). Type 9 is a credible third: role-flexible self-effacement (C14, C15, C72, C73), his 2026 account of uncertainty, a weak sense of self and avoided hard conversations (C39, C110), and the fear of harming relationships in the 2017 email (C25). It fails to explain his pushing onto the language project over its leaders' objections, a harsh written critique, working around people, and his performer's history (C31–C33, C04, C05, C62). Type 6 (loyalty, team belonging, fear language, C80, C81, C101) is weaker because he shows little threat-scanning or doubt about authority and is publicly optimistic. Type 5 is undercut because he treats knowledge as instrumental ("I learn best when I have something specific in mind to build," C79) and leads publicly. Type 8 is undercut by his self-reported reluctance to confront Musk and to have hard conversations (C25, C39, C110). Type 2 is undercut by his celebrating being unneeded and leaving Stripe (C70, C13, C71). Wing and subtype are optional and omitted from the draft.
type_hypothesis.discriminator: When doing it the right way and winning or looking competent conflict, which does he protect, and how does he justify his own reversals? A Type 1 should hold process and principle at a cost to speed and frame reversals as correcting a wrong. Brockman's record leans the other way: a launch rule built around shipping (C66), a former colleague's "ends-over-means" and "work around people" (C33), a peer review that attacked a colleague's "bureaucratic processes" rather than defending procedure (C32), a trial gloss that the 2017 move "would actually serve the mission" but be hard to face "in the mirror" (C23), and a PAC reversal justified by how it was "reflecting on the company" and distracting staff, not by calling the giving wrong (C106, C107). His one documented competence crisis was organized around visible results and others' estimate of him ("nothing to show," correcting people who rated him highly) and resolved only where failure felt "ok" and private (C53, C17, C54, C80, C84, C85), which is the 3 fear of failing in view rather than the 1 fear of being wrong (C86). Limits: several discriminating items are anonymous (C33), reported by rivals (C32), relayed through a second outlet (C106), or are testimony with legal incentives (C23); the mirror idiom also fits a One's conscience. The discriminator rests on convergence with the 2019 essay (C109), not on any single item.
type_hypothesis.unexplained: The moral vocabulary itself (C89, C35, C52) is not fully dissolved by the 3 reading; neither is the depth of his emotion about followers' loyalty (C36, C119) or the repeated willingness to drop status roles and do grunt work (C10, C70, C72, C73). The jointly written 2017 confession of fearing to confront Musk (C25) and his own 2026 account of indecision (C39, C110) fit 9 better than 3. The "Happy to not become rich... so long as no one else is" line (C22) mixes fairness and comparison and has no single reading. November 17, 2023 (C35, C101, C102) favors a One or Six more than a Three. The inner motive for his political donations is unknown (C41, C108; WIRED not opened). The content of the Sutskever memo (C34, C96) is unresolved. Disputed accounts not used in the draft ("money and power," the "countries plan") remain in the research record only.
